moveDecisions.rationale: The definition, examples, and attribute conflict are clearly recoverable, while describing the classical position as denying genuinely gratuitous evil is broadly fair but somewhat compressed.

The evil-God parity and possibility-versus-probability warrant materially advance the subsidiary burden, though the symmetry and rival explanations remain insufficiently defended for exceptional ratings.

The disagreement-to-irrationality route is clear but leaves a material bridge from doctrinal diversity to conflict with divine love, while its sweeping claims about most theists and universalism are poorly qualified.

The salvation-hoop analogy intelligibly develops a necessary subsidiary burden, but its empirical support is mostly asserted and its universal punishment framing omits decisive theological qualifications.
The inferential route is understandable, but materially unstable use of atheism, physicalism, and unguided processes weakens precision and reconstructs the opposing position too narrowly.

The survival-versus-truth distinction is recoverable but stated with imprecise necessity, while limiting the claim to atheistic naturalism makes the representation fairer despite an omitted truth-behavior connection.

The move directly advances the fine-tuning subsidiary bridge and is clearly stated, but omits probability measures and rival hypotheses, making its practical-impossibility claim markedly overconfident.
The move clearly states the moral-law dilemma and directly establishes a necessary subsidiary burden, but does not itself complete a central or motion-level route.

This is an untested summary of the speaker's own cumulative case, so the false-and-75 charity pair applies; the summary reaches the motion but compresses aggregation, divine identity, suffering, and supporting warrants.

The reply contacts the naturalism conflation and the survival-versus-truth premise but leaves the positive theistic reliability claim unanswered; unsupported sociological assertions and an overstated reconstruction weaken the other dimensions.

The reply contacts the claim that selection can favor broadly accurate cognition because false representations may be costly, but leaves unanswered the separate guided-evolution claim that a creator intends rational knowers; its cost claim is insufficiently supported and qualified.

The reply contacts the asserted correlation between evolutionary success and truth but leaves unanswered that broad, imperfect reliability may suffice; it advances the exact bridge while assuming divine truth-directed intent and unnamed counterexamples.

The reply identifies alleged dependence on divinely implanted cognition and states the defeating consequence that a shared reliability problem cannot favor theism; however, equating mysterious purposes with cognitive unreliability is underwarranted and overstates the represented position.

The concession contacts suffering's evidential force but leaves gratuitousness and the divine-attribute conflict unanswered; the selected span supplies little warrant beyond acknowledging the problem.

The move supplies contrary material about Christian normativity but leaves both apparent gratuitousness and incompatibility with divine attributes unanswered; conflating atheism with moral nihilism undermines its inference, warrant, calibration, and precision.

Afterlife restoration is relevant contrary material but contacts neither whether suffering serves a greater purpose nor whether gratuitous evil conflicts with the stated attributes; compensation is clearly expressed yet does not logically supply justification.

Naming respected theodicies and divine solidarity contacts neither the evidential probability of gratuitous evil nor the evil-God parity objection; the content is understandable but relies on authority and theological promises with inadequate qualification.

The evolutionary account explains the origin and emotional force of moral intuitions but does not contact whether atheism can affirm their normative truth; reducing that target to a causal-explanation demand weakens its representation.

The reply diagnoses that generic creator arguments do not identify the all-powerful, all-loving God and states the defeating motion-level consequence; its route is clear, though it compresses the positive case's personal and moral qualifications.

The dilemma identifies both dependence and arbitrariness defects and separately states why either defeats divine moral grounding; sweeping scriptural examples and categorical conclusions remain underqualified and only moderately warranted.

The historical-influence claim contacts neither horn of the divine-command dilemma nor whether the cited commands are moral, though it is issue-bearing contrary material; its causal historical certainty substantially exceeds the supplied warrant.
The reply explicitly reconstructs both horns and answers them with goodness grounded in God's nature, making the two-component full-answer tuple and the clearer precision rating appropriate.
The reply identifies the alleged defect that grounding goodness in God's nature merely restates the horns and gives the defeating consequence, but largely asserts rather than defends that collapse.

The move clearly and fairly contrasts pre-evolutionary design inference with convergent evolutionary explanation, directly advancing the subsidiary bridge; unspecified evidence and categorical claims about what evolution establishes require lower calibration.
